title: Galactic Cherry Blossom
caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 1156, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 1156 looks like a cherry tree in blossom. Its many bright blooms are stellar nurseries, where new stars are forming. Energetic light from the newborn stars streams out and strikes nearby pockets of hydrogen gas, which then glows with a characteristic pink color.

The galaxy lies in the constellation Aries, the Ram. It is classed as a dwarf irregular galaxy, meaning it lacks a clear spiral or rounded shape and is fairly small. Even so, its central region is relatively large and more crowded with stars.

In NGC 1156, some pockets of gas spin the opposite way from the rest of the galaxy. That hints at a close encounter with another galaxy at some point in its past. The other galaxy's gravity, and the turmoil of the encounter, could have scrambled what was probably once a more orderly rotation, leaving the odd motion seen today.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1156 in red visible light at 625 nm and through a narrow filter at 658 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The narrow filter isolates the glow of gas in star-forming regions, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.
